title: The Disaster at Isandlwana
text:
In January 1879 the British invaded the Zulu kingdom of King Cetshwayo. The main column under Lord Chelmsford camped below a rocky hill called Isandlwana. The British commanders were confident that their rifles and artillery would beat any Zulu attack, and their main fear was that the Zulu army would avoid battle.

The camp was not fortified. No wagon laager was formed and no trenches were dug, partly because the column expected to move on soon. Early on 22 January, reports came of Zulu forces to the southeast. Chelmsford took about half his column out to find and fight them, leaving the camp under Lieutenant Colonel Henry Pulleine, later joined by Colonel Anthony Durnford.

The main Zulu army, more than twenty thousand men, was in fact hidden in a valley a few miles away from the camp. Discovered by a British patrol, it attacked at once in the traditional formation, with horns sweeping around both flanks. The British firing line was spread too thin and far from the camp, and it was outflanked. Within a few hours the camp was overrun. About 1,300 men of the British force died, among the worst defeats the British army suffered at the hands of an indigenous force.

Chelmsford returned that evening to find the camp destroyed. The British won the war later in 1879, but Isandlwana shook the Empire's sense of invincibility.
lesson: Contempt for an opponent leads to skipped precautions and divided strength. Plan as if the other side is as capable as you are.
people: Lord Chelmsford, Henry Pulleine, Anthony Durnford, Cetshwayo
source: Proceedings of the Court of Inquiry into the loss of the camp at Isandlwana (1879); Ian Knight, Zulu Rising (2010)
